The filings analyzed, among other things, the performance of the EmPOWER 
Utilities’ and DHCD’s portfolios for the second half of the 2025 program year as well as 
the progress made by several work groups on Commission directives. The hearing allowed 
the parties to provide additional testimony to the Commission on various aspects of the 
2024-2026 EmPOWER program cycle, as well as the upcoming 2027-2029 program cycle. 
After considering the filings, testimony, and requests presented, the Commission notes the 
semi-annual filings and makes the determinations and directives provided herein. 
Goal Setting for the 2027-2029 Program Cycle 
In Order No. 92176, issued February 6, 2026, the Commission approved a 
methodology to establish lifecycle greenhouse gas (“GHG”) reduction goals for 2026-
2029. The approved methodology was a consensus proposal except for an adder that would 
have established a longer estimated useful life (“EUL”), such that the goal would be higher.

On May 12, 2026, Governor Wes Moore signed into law the Utility Reducing 
Energy Load Inflation for Everyday Family Act (“the Utility RELIEF Act”)40 which, 
among many things, modifies the EmPOWER Maryland statute as follows: 
(1) 
Removal of gas utilities from the EmPOWER 
programs; 

(2) 
Reduction of the original 2.5% goal to 1.75% from 
2027 – 2029, 2.0% from 2030 – 2023, 2.25% from 
2033 – 2035, and 2.5% each year on and after 2036; 
and 

(3) 
Allows solar to count toward the goal up to 20 
percent. 

While the Future Programming Work Group filed a report on April 15, 2026 to 
address issues related to the previously established goal, the work group’s subsequent filing 
on May 22, 2026 addressed the need to modify the goal in response to the Utility RELIEF 
Act, and noted that all parties agreed to utilize an updated marginal emission rate provided 
by the Maryland Department of the Environment (“MDE”).41 The filing contained four 
different positions from the parties as to how to modify previously approved goal values, 
including changes to the previous consensus methodology. All methodologies accounted 
for the reduced goal values; where the methodologies diverged was the treatment of the 
EUL to transform the energy targets into lifecycle GHG reduction goals. 
Staff and MDE proposed using the same methodology previously approved in 
Order No. 92176, but adjusting the EUL bin weighting to exclude conservation voltage 
reduction (“CVR”), as that program will not be part of the next program cycle.42 In support 
of its position, Staff notes that if only behind-the-meter programs were considered in 2025,

The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (“ACEEE”), with the 
support of MEEA, OPC, Montgomery County, and GHHI, proposes keeping the consensus 
methodology approved in Order No. 92176 to bin EULs, but adjusted for a different 
average marginal emissions rate that also updates annually, and including distributed solar 
in the EUL bin weighting to reflect the recent allowance of distributed solar toward 20% 
of the statutory goal.45 
Potomac Edison, the Joint Maryland Exelon Utilities, and MEA support reverting 
to the methodology in place for 2025 and 2026, which uses the average statewide 2025 
EUL. They claim the approved EUL bin weighted methodology from Order No. 92176 is 
“misaligned with the expected goal reduction in the Utility RELIEF Act” and argue that a 
higher EUL predicated on the removal of CVR “conteract[s] and circumvents the 
EmPOWER goal reductions established by the Act.”46 They argue that their proposal is 
more realistic, consistent with the methodology for 2025-2026, “maintains the expectation

The Commission acknowledges that, while it has already established a goal for the 
2027-2029 program cycle, recent modifications to the EmPOWER statute necessitate a 
change to the approved goal. The Commission expects the utilities and DHCD to have 
already been developing their plans. 
At issue among the proposals is how to arrive at an appropriate EUL. Unlike the 
previously approved goal, parties are in disagreement as to how the 2027-2029 goal should 
be established. The original near-consensus EUL that the non-utility parties generally 
continue to support with modifications, was premised upon the statewide projected 2025-
2026 utility program plans EULs with the removal of combined heat and power (“CHP”) 
and CVR. The utility supported EUL of 7 is based upon the results on their program 
performance in 2025 but used differently in their calculations to derive their different goal 
proposals. The utilities have not challenged the validity of the previously used 
methodology, just that the outcome results in a goal value that they allege does not align 
with the General Assembly’s intent behind revising the EmPOWER statute. 

While the EULs proposed by the parties are all rooted in historical project design 
or execution, the Commission notes that the goal and the inputs, including EUL, are tools 
to determine what future utility program plans should be. The Commission need not be 
locked into previous program design to set the goal, though it is a useful tool in establishing

reasonable benchmarks for goal setting. The Commission directs the utilities to include 
two goals for consideration in their upcoming program proposal filings. 
First, the Commission directs the utilities to develop an EmPOWER portfolio based 
on the methodology proposed by Staff and MDE. This is the only proposal that appears to 
closely mirror the Commission’s previous authorization, with updates for the revised 
statute and more recently available marginal emissions values. The Commission believes 
there is some merit to the proposal put forward by ACEEE regarding the calculation and 
application of the average marginal emissions rate that should be considered in future goal 
setting, as it may lead to more accurate results. At this time, the Commission is not 
persuaded to incorporate an adjustment to the weighting of the goal calculation for the 
potential inclusion of solar. As noted, the weighting of EUL in the non-utility methodology 
establishes the goal, which in turn leads to the final value that the utilities will build their 
program plans around. Whether the utility will use solar or another similarly long-lived 
measure to achieve the goal does not necessarily dictate what size the goal should be. The 
use of solar, or any other measure, for that matter, will determine how much of the goal is 
satisfied. Additionally, the use of solar to count towards the goal is permissible for only 
one cycle and is not a permanent fixture in the program. 
Second, the Commission directs the utilities to develop plans based on a goal where 
the weighted average EUL is at least 7. Concerns about the on-going cost of the 
EmPOWER Program warrant consideration, and since it is unclear what the cost of the 
next cycle will be when establishing these goals, the Commission believes it is prudent to 
consider a range of outcomes that satisfy goal establishment. Therefore, the Commission 
will also examine a portfolio based on a weighted average EUL of 7. The Commission 

10 
notes that if Staff’s methodology is re-weighted such that a 100 percent of the weighting is 
an EUL of 7, this appears to produce similar results to the methodology proposed by 
Potomac Edison, the Joint Maryland Exelon Utilities, and MEA.55 Therefore, Staff shall 
provide the results of its methodology but re-weighting the goal to 100 percent EUL of 7 
within 5 days of the issuance of this Order. While SMECO’s approach tries to adhere to 
the previously authorized methodology, it uses a simple ratio to make an adjustment instead 
of a re-weighting. 
Additionally, the law requires that, when establishing a goal, the Commission must 
consider the most recent MDE plan to meet the State’s climate goals.56 This was not 
discussed as part of the utilities’ request to modify the previously authorized methodology 
and the resulting EUL to reflect 2025 plan results. The Utilities shall therefore explain 
explicitly how the 7-year EUL is in alignment with the plan versus the EUL of 9.6. With 
regard to the disagreement among the parties as to how much more the Staff position will 
cost relative to the utility positions, the Utilities shall, for each program, provide detailed 
data and descriptions as to the drivers of the cost differences in their respective program 
filing.

Pepco and Delmarva Budget Reallocation Requests 
Pepco and Delmarva individually request the Commission’s approval for certain 
budget reallocations that exceed the 15 percent budget flexibility granted to the utilities in 
Order No. 90957.59 Pepco’s request is made in response to higher than anticipated customer 
participation in its Midstream Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (“HVAC”), 
Small Business, and Commercial Midstream Programs, which are projected to exceed their 
approved budgets prior to the end of the 2024-2026 program cycle.60 Pepco is therefore 
requesting a transfer of $7,065,420 from its Home Performance with ENERGY STAR 
Program to its Midstream HVAC Program in order to allow the Midstream Program to not 
only continue, but to continue with increased incentive levels to maximize current-cycle 
incentive expenditures and accelerate the delivery of energy savings and GHG 
reductions.”61 
Within its C&I portfolio, Pepco is requesting approval to reallocate $13,700,000 
from the Prescriptive Program, $3,000,000 from the Custom Program, and $4,000,000 
from the Retro-commissioning Program to provide $15,000,000 to its Small Business 
Program and $5,700,000 to its Commercial Midstream Program.62 Pepco states that the 
programs to receive funds have experienced strong participation and rapid growth, both of 
which are expected to continue. Conversely, the programs from which funds would be 
transferred have had lower incentive spend than anticipated and are not forecasted to fully 
utilize their current cycle budget.63

interpretation of Public Utilities Article (“PUA”) § 7-224(a)(2) of the Annotated Code of 
Maryland as it pertains to the GHG reduction goals for DHCD programs, the Commission 
determined that, under the statute, DHCD’s required goal is to achieve a minimum 
aggregate savings of 0.9 percent of the electric and gas sales of eligible low-income

a proposal to achieve its interpretation of the statutory goal of 0.9 percent in the aggregate 
as well as the work group’s interpretation of the statutory goal of 0.9 percent annually.”67 
On May 6, 2026, DHCD filed a request for an extension of the deadline by which
